chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hashim from Salim ibn Mukram from Sa'd al-Iskaf, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about the 'qaramil' (hair extensions/extensions), which women make in their heads, attaching them to their hair. He said, 'There is no harm in it for the woman as long as she adorns herself with it for her husband.' I said, 'It reached us that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) cursed the al-wasilah (one who extends) and the al-mawsulah (the one who is extended).' He said, 'Not there; rather, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) cursed the al-wasilah who committed fornication in her youth, and when she grew old, she led the women to the men; that is the al-wasilah and the al-mawsulah.'

key_terms.الْقَرَامِلِ: Hair extensions or artificial hair pieces worn by women
key_terms.الْوَاصِلَةَ: The one who extends (referring to hair or a specific type of woman)
key_terms.لِزَوْجِهَا: For her husband (context of permissible adornment)
key_terms.وَالْمَوْصُولَةَ: The one who is extended (the counterpart to the wasilah)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the hair extensions worn by women and the 'al-wasilah' cursed by the Prophet?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration to distinguish between the general practice of hair extension (qaramil) for marital adornment and the specific 'wasilah' cursed in other traditions, whom scholars identify as a promiscuous woman who later guided others. This clarification highlights the Shia method of reconciling apparent contradictions by contextualizing the object of the curse rather than the act itself. It underscores the principle that adornment for one's spouse is permissible unless it leads to broader moral corruption.
